clue.text: Senses uncivil rioting – the participation of everybody? (13)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters — exactly the enumeration

explanation.walkthrough: A long anagram hides best when its fodder reads as an opinion rather than a bag of letters, and 'Senses uncivil' does. Counting the fodder against the (13) is what breaks it open.
explanation.definitionFit: the participation of everybody → INCLUSIVENESS: the abstract noun for the policy of leaving nobody out, rather than any single act of including someone.

clue.text: North American cheers most of experiment involving old swimming pools (9)

blocks.note: NA is the standard abbreviation for North American
'cheers' in its thank-you sense is TA
a TRIAL is an experiment, and 'most of' drops its last letter
o = old, one of the workhorse crossword abbreviations

explanation.walkthrough: A natatorium is a building put up around an indoor pool, and its plural swaps the Latin -um for -a, the same way stadium goes to stadia.
explanation.definitionFit: swimming pools → NATATORIA: the Latin plural of natatorium, the formal architectural word for a hall built around a pool.

clue.text: Composer’s inclination for radio broadcast? (5)

blocks.note: a ship's list is its inclination

explanation.walkthrough: Franz Liszt's surname is pronounced 'list' in English, so a foreign name is being reached through an ordinary English word. The nautical sense of list, a lean to one side, is the one to bank.
explanation.definitionFit: Composer → LISZT: definition by example, one composer standing for the whole trade, which is what the question mark at the end is admitting.

clue.text: Hidden material – timber under stone (5)

blocks.note: st is the abbreviation for stone, the imperial weight
ash is a hardwood, so it answers to timber

explanation.walkthrough: 'Under' places a piece further down the grid, so in a down entry the word named first ends up second. Expect that inversion whenever a down clue says under, below or supporting.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidden material → STASH: a stash is a quantity of something squirrelled away out of sight, so the definition names the concealment and the goods at once.

clue.text: Malevolent, grabbing a lot of power at second hand (9)

blocks.note: vicious = malevolent, and it opens up to take the other piece
arm carries the sense of might — the arm of the law — and 'a lot of' keeps all but its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Power' for ARM is the muscular sense: the arm of the law, force of arms. That equation is the piece of vocabulary the clue is really testing.
explanation.definitionFit: at second hand → VICARIOUS: a vicarious thrill is one felt through somebody else's experience, which is exactly what having it second hand means.

clue.text: Mention Australian mechanics – something audacious about that (9)

blocks.note: neck is brass nerve — 'you've got some neck' — and it splits to wrap the rest
A is the abbreviation for Australian
mech is the short form of mechanics

explanation.walkthrough: Neck for nerve is slang worth keeping. The 'that' is the setter pointing back at words already used rather than introducing anything new, which is how a short clue can afford two pieces of wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Mention → NAMECHECK: to namecheck somebody is to mention them by name in public, so the answer is a narrower, broadcast-flavoured version of the plain verb.

clue.text: Travelled in winter, perhaps raised aloft (5)

blocks.note: the winter-sports verb: to ski is to travel on skis
in cricket, to sky a ball is to hit it steeply into the air

explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' is honest labelling: skiing is only one way of travelling in winter. Both halves are past tenses of verbs, which is the join a double definition always needs.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are the same past tense: to ski across snow, and to sky a ball high in cricket, spelled SKIED either way.

clue.text: Adventurous types in middle of Hawkins – broadcast of Stranger Things two-thirds complete (7,6)

blocks.note: HAWKINS has seven letters, so its middle one is K
STRANGER in full, then two-thirds of THINGS — four of its six letters

explanation.walkthrough: Hawkins is the town Stranger Things is set in, so the surface is one thought while the wordplay treats the two halves separately. A fraction of a word is rare enough to be worth counting twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Adventurous types → KNIGHTS ERRANT: a knight errant wandered in search of adventure, so the plural names that particular breed of roving adventurer.

clue.text: The writer’s supporting Minister (mostly) about relationship and scandalous behaviours (13)

blocks.note: the setter writing as himself: the writer's = I'M
pro means in favour of, so supporting
a priest is a minister, and 'mostly' drops the last letter
a tie is a bond or relationship, and it goes inside

explanation.walkthrough: 'The writer' is the setter talking about himself, one of a small family of first-person conventions: it yields I, I'M or ME depending on what the apostrophe is doing.
explanation.definitionFit: scandalous behaviours → IMPROPRIETIES: an impropriety is a breach of what is proper, and the plural names the individual acts rather than the quality.

clue.text: Exclamation of success after recalling devil woman? (7)

blocks.note: Satan is the devil, written backwards by 'recalling'
'Ha!' is the cry of triumph

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark is doing real work: a name can only ever be an example of 'woman', so the setter has to flag it. Satan backwards is a device you will meet again.
explanation.definitionFit: woman → NATASHA: definition by example, a Russian given name standing in for the whole category, which the question mark politely admits.

clue.text: Tramp beside Cambridge river taking in one feature of arboreal growth (7)

blocks.note: the Cam runs through Cambridge
a bum is a tramp, and it opens to take the next piece
the Roman numeral one

explanation.walkthrough: The Cam is the crossword's default river, turning up whenever Cambridge or its university is mentioned, and 'bum' for tramp is the American register the surface quietly borrows.
explanation.definitionFit: feature of arboreal growth → CAMBIUM: the thin layer of dividing cells under the bark, the tissue that actually makes a tree thicker each year.

clue.text: Mean for one to return rubbish (3,2)

blocks.note: 'for one' is e.g., turned round by 'to return'
tat is cheap rubbish

explanation.walkthrough: 'For one' is the everyday way of saying e.g., and an abbreviation is fair game to reverse — two letters are as reversible as ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean → GET AT: the 'what are you getting at?' sense, where the phrasal verb asks what somebody intends to say rather than what they are reaching for.

clue.text: Woman’s concealing a way with detectives and juice (4,5)

blocks.note: the woman's = her, and it splits to hide the rest
the clue's own 'a', taken at face value
rd = road, the crossword's usual way
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department

explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman's' is asking for the possessive HER rather than a noun, a small grammatical step that is easy to miss while the surface reads as somebody hiding something.
explanation.definitionFit: juice → HARD CIDER: cider is pressed apple juice, and in North America 'hard' marks the fermented version, so the definition names the drink by its raw material.

clue.text: Light bit of rest in hospital bed rejected (5)

blocks.note: H is the map-and-crossword abbreviation for hospital
a cot is a bed; behind the H it makes HCOT, which 'rejected' turns round
'bit of' takes the first letter of rest

explanation.walkthrough: Note the scope of 'rejected': it turns the whole hospital bed round, not just the bed. An instruction at the end of a clue reaches back over everything the phrase covers.
explanation.definitionFit: Light → TORCH: in British usage a torch is the handheld electric lamp you carry in the dark, so the definition is the everyday noun rather than a flame.

clue.text: Source of heavy band equipment on charter in southern county (9)

blocks.note: the first letter of heavy
amps are what a band plugs into
to charter a boat or coach is to hire it

explanation.walkthrough: 'Source of' is one of the quiet indicators — no shuffling, no hiding, just the head of the word — and 'charter' is wanted as a verb here, not as a document.
explanation.definitionFit: southern county → HAMPSHIRE: definition by example, since Hampshire is one of several counties along England's south coast rather than the only one.

clue.text: Fascist movement? Sees to changes among Republicans (5,4)

blocks.note: the GOP is the Grand Old Party, and it splits to hold the anagram
the letters of SEES TO, rearranged by 'changes'

explanation.walkthrough: GOP for the Republicans is American shorthand a British puzzle assumes you know, and the surface — Republicans making changes — is where all the misdirection sits.
explanation.definitionFit: Fascist movement → GOOSE STEP: the stiff-legged parade march adopted by fascist armies, so 'movement' means a way of moving rather than a political faction.

clue.text: Something that makes classes rushed? Not entirely (9)

blocks.note: genera are biological classes, the plural of genus
tore is rushed, and 'Not entirely' leaves the last letter off

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not entirely' sits at the end but only reaches back to 'rushed': a trimming instruction takes the word beside it, never the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that makes → GENERATOR: an agent noun, where the -or ending names a machine by the job it does, here turning fuel or steam into electricity.

clue.text: Coaches? Coaches left after I disembarked (9)

definitions.note: 'Coaches' is plural and the answer a mass noun; the question mark marks definition by example, coaches being one kind of it rather than a synonym.

blocks.note: the second Coaches is railway carriages, TRAINS, with the I stepping off
port is the left-hand side of a ship
the letter taken out: I leaves TRAINS

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is one word doing opposite jobs: the first Coaches defines, the second is rolling stock. Repeating a word like that is a legitimate device, not a slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Coaches? → TRANSPORT: definition by example, coaches being one form of the uncountable noun for the moving of people and goods.

clue.text: Mean types ruined online transactions (1-8)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, nine letters

explanation.walkthrough: The enumeration is the tell: (1-8) means one letter, a hyphen and an eight-letter word, and in a modern crossword that opening letter is nearly always the e- of email or e-commerce.
explanation.definitionFit: online transactions → E-PAYMENTS: money moving over the internet, with the e- prefix carrying the 'online' half and the noun the transaction half.

clue.text: Book launch finally having a lot of similar military material (5)

blocks.note: the last letters of Book and launch
akin means similar, and 'a lot of' keeps all but its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally' can harvest the last letter of every word in front of it, not just one. Reading it as a plural instruction is what makes the opening pair available.
explanation.definitionFit: military material → KHAKI: the dust-coloured cloth armies have uniformed in since India in the 1840s, so the definition names a fabric by who wears it.

clue.text: Relieved apprehension in various readers about The Guardian’s volte-face (9)

blocks.note: the letters of readers, shuffled by 'various'
the paper printing the puzzle is US, and a volte-face turns it about

explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian calling itself 'us' is the setter winking at the paper the puzzle appears in — a trick every publication's crossword allows itself, and one to watch for in the Times too.
explanation.definitionFit: Relieved apprehension → REASSURED: to reassure somebody is precisely to take their fear away, and the two-word definition matches the verb's past tense.

clue.text: Excuse a sexual impulse, but not act (5)

blocks.note: the clue's own 'a', taken at face value
LIBIDO is the sexual impulse, with two letters removed
act = DO, and DO is the pair of letters coming off LIBIDO

explanation.walkthrough: The deletion works on a word the clue never spells out and removes another it only hints at, so you have to reach LIBIDO and read 'act' as DO before anything can be trimmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Excuse → ALIBI: strictly a plea of having been somewhere else, but everyday use has widened it to any excuse offered for one's conduct.

clue.text: Italian writer not ultimately hosted by another European (5)

blocks.note: a Dane is another European, and here the host word
'ultimately' takes the last letter of not

explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' is raw material here rather than a negative, which is the trap. 'Ultimately' always means the final letter of the word beside it and never the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian writer → DANTE: definition by example, Dante Alighieri of the Divine Comedy being the Italian a five-letter space is usually after.

clue.text: Where many maps show Alaska and Hawaii? This month around Spain (5)

definitions.text: Where many maps show Alaska and Hawaii?

blocks.note: inst. is the old commercial abbreviation for the current month
E is Spain's international vehicle code, from España

explanation.walkthrough: Two abbreviations to bank here: inst for the present month, still lurking in old business letters, and E for Spain from the plate on the back of the car.
explanation.definitionFit: An INSET is the small boxed map dropped into a corner of a larger one, exactly how atlases fit Alaska and Hawaii beside the mainland.

clue.text: One heartless sod is stupid (5)

definitions.note: 'Stupid' is an adjective and the answer a noun; the setter leans on the way English uses this particular noun attributively — an idiot grin, idiot boy — where the two are interchangeable.

indicators.note: the heart of DIVOT is its middle letter V, and that is what goes

blocks.note: the Roman numeral one
a divot is a sod of turf, minus the letter at its centre

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sod' is turf here rather than an insult — a divot is the lump a golfer digs out of the grass — and 'heartless' always means the middle letter leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: stupid → IDIOT: the noun names a person by the quality, the way 'fool' does, so an adjective can stand in for somebody who has it.

clue.text: Note excellent view, largely ingenuous (7)

blocks.note: n. is the standard written abbreviation for note
A1 means first-rate, and the crossword spells its numeral as the letter I
a VISTA is a view, and 'largely' keeps all but its last letter

explanation.walkthrough: A1 written as AI is the convention worth banking: whenever a clue says excellent or top-notch, expect the numeral one to be doing duty as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: ingenuous → NAIVIST: the adjective belongs to naive art, the deliberately unschooled and wide-eyed manner, so it carries the same open innocence.

clue.text: Offensive is torpedoing rotating satellite close to home (7)

blocks.note: the clue's own 'is' joins the fodder
a moon is a natural satellite, and it supplies the bulk of the letters
'close to' takes the last letter of home

explanation.walkthrough: Noisome has nothing to do with noise: it means foul or offensive, and comes from the same root as annoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Offensive → NOISOME: noisome describes something, usually a smell, so foul that it offends the senses rather than merely displeasing you.

clue.text: Maine – Eastern and petite, possibly (4,4,5)

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 13 letters

explanation.walkthrough: With thirteen letters to place, working out what sort of phrase you are building matters more than the letters themselves — and American state nicknames are fair game in a British cryptic.
explanation.definitionFit: Maine → PINE TREE STATE: the state's official nickname, taken from the white pine that stands on both its flag and its seal.
